Non-discretionary bonuses, shift differentials and commissions are spread across the hours they were earned in, which raises it. This number appears on no document a worker receives, and getting it wrong is the single most common error in wage arithmetic.
California pays 1.5x for hours over eight in a single workday, regardless of the weekly total. Most of the country has no such rule, so payroll systems configured federally miss it.
California pays 2x for hours over twelve in a single workday. A thirteen-hour shift contains one double-time hour that a federal payroll configuration will price at straight time.
1.5x for straight-time hours over forty in a workweek. Hours already paid as daily overtime are not counted a second time.

Paying the same hour twice, once as daily overtime and again as weekly. It is not allowed, and it is the error that inflates a damages figure and gets the whole model excluded. Backpay refuses to pyramid and says so in its output.
Working seven days in one workweek pays 1.5x for the first eight hours of the seventh day and 2x beyond, no matter how few hours the week held in total.
An unpaid thirty-minute break that must begin before the end of the fifth hour, and a second before the end of the tenth. A missed, late or short one owes an hour of pay at the regular rate.
A paid ten-minute break per four hours worked, or major fraction of four. Major fraction means strictly more than two hours, which is why a six-hour shift owes one rest period and not two.
The one hour of pay at the regular rate owed for each workday with a missed meal period, and separately for each with a missed rest period. Two separate premiums, capped at one of each per day.

A worker needs to know whether one paycheck was short. A law firm needs the same computation run across two hundred workers and four years, in a form an opposing expert can attack and a judge can follow.

No, and it will not act like one. It does arithmetic and cites the section behind each figure. Whether you have a claim worth bringing is a question for a lawyer, and the answer depends on facts arithmetic cannot see.

blocks.body:
It is arithmetic. It multiplies your hours by the rate California required and names the section that says so, and it will tell you when the answer comes out right, which is worth knowing too.

pages.title: How Backpay works
pages.description: Four steps from a stack of pay stubs to a damages schedule where every figure names the Labor Code section that produced it. What the engine sees, and what it refuses to guess at.

blocks.lede: Four steps, and one of them is the engine refusing to answer.

blocks.h2: From a stack of stubs to a schedule

items.name: Give it the hours and the pay
items.text: A worker types in one week. A firm imports a payroll export covering hundreds of people and four years. Same engine either way, different loop.

items.name: It works out the regular rate first
items.text: Before any overtime hour can be priced, the rate has to be right. Non-discretionary bonuses, shift differentials and commissions get apportioned across the hours they were earned in. This step is where most hand-built spreadsheets go wrong, and the error is invisible on the stub.

items.name: It classifies every hour, and refuses to double-count
items.text: Daily overtime over eight, double time over twelve, weekly overtime over forty straight-time hours, and the seventh-consecutive-day rule on top. Hours already paid as daily overtime are not counted again as weekly. That rule against pyramiding is what separates a defensible model from an inflated one.

items.name: It prices the premiums, then shows its work
items.text: One hour of pay for each day with a missed meal period, separately for each with a missed rest period. Then every line comes back with the section number behind it, so the arithmetic can be checked rather than believed.

blocks.body:
The engine stops and says so when the law does not fit the facts it was given. Four conditions do that: an alternative workweek schedule, a qualifying collective bargaining agreement, an exempt classification, and piece-rate pay. Each one changes the calculation in a way this engine does not model.

That refusal is a feature you can sell to a lawyer. An attorney will not sign a damages model they cannot trace, and an overstated claim does more damage than a missing one, because it is the thing an opposing expert attacks first and the reason a whole schedule gets excluded. A generic chatbot asked the same question will produce a confident number, pyramid the daily and weekly overtime, and cite a Labor Code section that does not exist.

blocks.h2: Why you cannot check this yourself
blocks.body:
The error is almost never in a number printed on your stub. It is in the rate those numbers were multiplied by.

California pays overtime on the regular rate, which is not the same as your hourly rate. If you got a production bonus, an attendance bonus, a shift differential or a commission, that money has to be spread across the hours you earned it in, and it raises the rate every overtime hour gets paid at. The regular rate appears on no document you receive. You cannot check a number you were never shown.

The Economic Policy Institute found the mechanism plainly: most workers do not recognise their pay is being shorted in the first place. Not that they lack the will to act, that they lack the number.

items.name: Overtime priced at the wrong rate
items.text: The commonest error, and the hardest to see. A bonus in the period changes what every overtime hour is worth.

items.name: Daily overtime missed entirely
items.text: California pays 1.5× over eight hours in a day, whatever the weekly total. Payroll set up for federal rules does not know that.

items.name: Double time not paid
items.text: Over twelve hours in one day is 2×. A thirteen-hour shift contains an hour most systems price at straight time.

items.name: The seventh day
items.text: Seven days in one workweek pays 1.5× for the first eight hours of the seventh, no matter how short the week was.

items.name: Meal and rest premiums
items.text: A missed, late or short break owes an hour of pay at the regular rate. Two separate premiums, and both are commonly ignored.

items.name: What is missing from the stub itself
items.text: California requires nine specific items on a wage statement. Missing ones carry penalties of their own, whether or not the pay was right.

blocks.h2: The part that matters in a deposition
blocks.body:
Every figure comes back with the section that produced it. Not a footnote at the bottom of the report, a citation on the line. When opposing counsel asks why an hour was priced at double time, the answer is Labor Code section 510(a) and the hour count that triggered it, on the same row.

And where the engine cannot model the facts, it returns a refusal instead of a number, naming the reason: an alternative workweek election, a collective bargaining agreement, piece-rate compensation, an exempt classification. A schedule that quietly guesses at any of those is a schedule that gets excluded.

pages.title: How Backpay is checked
pages.description: The engine has 24 tests, refuses four categories of input it cannot model, and was corrected twice by its own test suite before anyone saw it. What is measured, and what is not yet.

blocks.lede: An arithmetic tool that is confidently wrong is worse than no tool. Here is what has actually been tested, and what has not.

blocks.body:
The engine carries 24 tests. Two of them were written after the code and immediately failed, which is the reason to write them.

The first: the rest-period rule owes one break per four hours worked or major fraction of four, and a major fraction means strictly more than two hours. A six-hour shift therefore owes one rest period. The first implementation returned two. That error then cascaded into a false premium on a meal period that had been validly waived, so one arithmetic slip was producing two wrong numbers.

Both were fixed at the source rather than patched at the output. The tests that caught them are still in the suite and still run on every change.

rows: Daily overtime thresholds are set by the election, not by statute. Guessing at the schedule produces a number with no basis.
Statutory overtime rules can be displaced by the agreement. The agreement is the authority and the engine has not read it.
Whether the classification is correct is usually the disputed question in the matter. Arithmetic cannot settle it.
The regular rate and rest-period pay are computed on a different basis entirely.

blocks.h2: What has not been established yet
blocks.body:
Two things, stated plainly because a page like this is worthless if it only lists what went well.

The engine has been tested against constructed cases, not against a corpus of real payroll records with known-correct answers. Until that exists, no accuracy percentage will be published. When it does, the number will be a fraction rather than a percentage until the sample is large enough to support a decimal point, because at twenty cases one item moves the figure five points.

And the engine currently models California only. Every rule in it is a California rule, and a figure produced for another state would be arithmetic dressed as law.

pages.title: Glossary of California wage terms
pages.description: The California wage-and-hour terms that decide whether a paycheck was correct, defined plainly. Regular rate, pyramiding, major fraction, premium pay and the rest.

blocks.lede: Sixteen terms that decide whether a paycheck was right. Most of the money hides in the first one.

blocks.body:
Regular rate of pay

The hourly figure overtime is actually calculated from. It is not the base hourly rate. Non-discretionary bonuses, shift differentials and commissions are spread across the hours they were earned in, which raises it. This number appears on no document a worker receives, and getting it wrong is the single most common error in wage arithmetic.

Daily overtime

California pays 1.5x for hours over eight in a single workday, regardless of the weekly total. Most of the country has no such rule, so payroll systems configured federally miss it.

Double time

California pays 2x for hours over twelve in a single workday. A thirteen-hour shift contains one double-time hour that a federal payroll configuration will price at straight time.

Weekly overtime

1.5x for straight-time hours over forty in a workweek. Hours already paid as daily overtime are not counted a second time.

Pyramiding

Paying the same hour twice, once as daily overtime and again as weekly. It is not allowed, and it is the error that inflates a damages figure and gets the whole model excluded. Backpay refuses to pyramid and says so in its output.

Seventh consecutive day

Working seven days in one workweek pays 1.5x for the first eight hours of the seventh day and 2x beyond, no matter how few hours the week held in total.

Meal period

An unpaid thirty-minute break that must begin before the end of the fifth hour, and a second before the end of the tenth. A missed, late or short one owes an hour of pay at the regular rate.

Rest period

A paid ten-minute break per four hours worked, or major fraction of four. Major fraction means strictly more than two hours, which is why a six-hour shift owes one rest period and not two.

Premium pay

The one hour of pay at the regular rate owed for each workday with a missed meal period, and separately for each with a missed rest period. Two separate premiums, capped at one of each per day.

Wage statement

The itemised pay stub California requires, with nine specific items on it. Missing items carry their own penalties, independent of whether the pay itself was correct.

Alternative workweek

A schedule adopted by employee election, such as four ten-hour days, under which the daily overtime thresholds change. Backpay refuses to compute where one is in effect rather than guessing at the schedule.

Non-exempt

An employee entitled to overtime. Backpay models non-exempt employees only, and refuses where the worker is classified exempt, because the classification itself is the disputed question and not one arithmetic can settle.

Class period

The span of time a wage-and-hour class action covers. In California it commonly runs four years back under the unfair competition statute, which is why a $200 weekly shortfall becomes a six-figure claim.

Named plaintiff

The individual whose payroll records anchor a class action. Their damages model is computed first and in the most detail, because it is what gets checked line by line.

Wage theft

The general term for pay an employer owed and did not pay. It covers deliberate underpayment and payroll misconfiguration alike, and the arithmetic does not distinguish between them.

Non-discretionary bonus

A bonus promised in advance for meeting a target, as opposed to a surprise gift. It must be included in the regular rate. Production bonuses, attendance bonuses and piece incentives all qualify.

blocks.body:
The Department of Labor recovered $3.28 billion in back wages over thirteen years. Estimates of what is taken run between $40 and $60 billion a year. That combination describes an agency running fewer and larger cases. The small individual claim is what got squeezed out, and the small individual claim is almost always the one where nobody ever computed the number.

Backpay computes the number. It gives that away to the person it happened to, and sells the same arithmetic, at scale, to the firms who are the only realistic route from a wrong paycheck to money actually recovered.
